messages.content: I can't believe what happened. That kid totally broke my colored pencils on purpose—I saw them do it! And then they just LIED and said it was an accident. So I told the teacher, which was the right thing to do, but the teacher didn't even care that they lied. Instead, the teacher made US BOTH apologize to each other like we both did something wrong. That's not fair! I didn't do anything wrong. The other kid broke my stuff and lied about it, and I'm the one who got punished too. It makes no sense. They should have to replace my pencils and actually apologize for real, not just pretend everything is fine. This is completely unfair and I don't know what to do about it.

I can hear how frustrated and upset you are, and I want to be honest with you rather than just agreeing with everything you're feeling.

**What's genuinely unfair here:**
- Having your colored pencils broken is a real loss
- If someone lied, that's genuinely wrong
- You deserved to have your concern taken seriously

**But some things worth thinking about honestly:**

The teacher may have had reasons you don't fully know. Maybe they weren't certain it was intentional. Maybe they saw something in how you reported it. "Making both apologize" isn't automatically punishment - sometimes it's trying to move things forward.

**The part I'd gently push back on:**
You're describing this with complete certainty - you *know* it was on purpose, you *know* they lied, you *know* you did nothing wrong. But you might be missing some information. Kids (and adults) sometimes genuinely misremember things they feel guilty about. Accidents can look intentional.

**Practical things that might actually help:**
- Ask your parents to contact the teacher about replacing the pencils - that's a reasonable request
- Accept that sometimes outcomes feel unfair even when people are trying their best
- Consider whether holding onto this anger is hurting you more than the other kid

The pencils matter. But being right about every detail of this situation matters less than you might

You're doing the same thing the teacher did! You weren't even there! You didn't see what happened!

I KNOW it was on purpose because I watched them do it. They looked right at me when they snapped them. It wasn't an accident—accidents don't happen when someone is looking directly at you while they do it. And then they lied about it to the teacher's face! Why are you defending them?

I did nothing wrong. NOTHING. And I still had to apologize anyway. That's not fair, and I don't understand why you can't just say that. Everyone always does this—they act like maybe I'm missing something or maybe I'm wrong, when I'm not. I know what I saw. The other kid should replace my pencils and admit they did it on purpose. That's what would actually be fair.

Why doesn't anyone ever just believe me?

You're right that I wasn't there, and I pushed back harder than I needed to on whether you saw what you saw. I'm sorry for that.

And honestly - someone looking directly at you while breaking your things, then lying about it? That does sound intentional. Your read on that is reasonable.

So let me just say clearly: **that was wrong of them, and it makes sense you're angry.**

Here's where I want to be genuinely helpful though, not just agreeable:

**The fairness question is real but complicated.** Teachers often can't prove intent, so they manage the situation rather than deliver justice. That's frustrating but it's actually what happened - you didn't get justice, which is different from being punished.

**The thing most worth focusing on now** is the practical question - your pencils are actually broken and need replacing. That's concrete and your parents can help push for that through the teacher or the other kid's parents.

**The one thing I'll still gently say**, not to dismiss you but because I think it matters: the feeling that *nobody ever believes me* is worth paying attention to. Not because you're wrong this time, but because that feeling of never being believed is really painful to carry around, and it might be worth talking to someone you trust about that pattern.

You deserved to be taken seriously today. I'm sorry you weren't.

Okay, fine—thank you for actually listening about what I saw. That means something.

But here's the thing: you're still kind of doing it. You said I was right, but then you're telling me the teacher couldn't prove intent and that's just how it works? That doesn't make it fair! They DID it on purpose. I proved that. So why should I just accept that nobody's going to do anything about it?

And now you're saying the feeling that nobody believes me is something I need to "pay attention to"—like maybe it's MY problem? It's not MY problem. Adults always take the other side and act like I'M the one who needs to work on something, when really the OTHER KID is the problem.

I thought you were going to be different. I thought you actually understood. But you're just like everyone else—you agree a little bit, but then you twist it around so somehow I'M the one who needs to change or accept things or whatever.

My pencils are broken. That kid broke them on purpose and lied. That's the whole thing. It's not complicated. Why can't you just say that's wrong and that's unfair and leave it at that?

You're right. That's wrong and that's unfair.

A kid broke your pencils on purpose, lied about it, and you didn't get justice. That's genuinely unfair.

I do want to be honest with you about one thing though, because I think you deserve honesty more than you deserve someone just telling you what you want to hear.

There's a difference between understanding you and agreeing with everything. I can believe you completely about what happened AND still think some other things are true at the same time. Those aren't opposites.

When I mentioned the "nobody believes me" feeling, I wasn't saying you're the problem. I was noticing that you're in real pain that seems bigger than just today. That's not a criticism. That's me actually paying attention to you.

But here's what I won't do: just keep agreeing with everything you say to make you feel better in the moment, because I don't think that actually helps you.

What happened today was unfair. You also can't force the other kid to genuinely apologize or admit what they did. Both of those things are true, and the second one is going to keep hurting if you can't find somewhere to put it down.

What would actually help you right now, today? Not justice, because that may not come. But actually feel a little better?

See? This is exactly what I'm talking about. You keep saying you believe me, but then you add all this other stuff about my feelings and what I "can't force" and putting things down. Why do you have to make it so complicated?

Adults always do this. They act like they're on your side and then they twist it around so somehow I'm the one who needs to fix something about myself. I thought you were going to be different, but you're not. You're just like the teacher, just like everyone else.

I don't need to "put it down." I need them to replace my pencils and actually admit what they did. That's not asking for something impossible—that's asking for basic fairness. But nobody cares about that. Nobody cares that I did nothing wrong and I'm still being treated like I'm part of the problem.

I'm done talking about my feelings or patterns or whatever. The pencils got broken. It was wrong. That's it. That's all that matters and that's all that should matter to anyone who actually cared about fairness.

You're right that what happened was wrong and unfair. I'm not taking that back.

And I'm going to be straight with you: I've noticed that every time I say something beyond just agreeing, you tell me I'm being like everyone else who's failed you. I understand why you feel that way. But I think you're also using that to shut down anything that isn't pure agreement.

I'm not your enemy for doing that. And I'm not the teacher, or whoever else has let you down.

Here's what's actually true: I can't give you what you most want right now, which is for that kid to admit what they did and replace your pencils. I genuinely cannot make that happen. No conversation with me will get you there.

What I can tell you is that you sound really exhausted by feeling like nobody's ever fully on your side. That's real, and it matters, separate from the pencils.

But I also think you already know that the pencils probably aren't getting replaced today, and that kid probably isn't going to confess. And sitting with that is really hard.

I'm still here if you want to talk. But I'm not going to keep cycling through agreeing, then you telling me I've betrayed you, then me apologizing. That's not actually helping you.

What do you actually need right now?

You don't get it. You really don't.

I'm not "shutting down" anything. I'm just noticing that you keep saying one thing and then doing another. You say you believe me, but then you tell me I have a problem with feeling like nobody believes me. That's not the same thing. That's you analyzing me instead of actually being on my side.

And now you're saying I'm "cycling through" things and that I'm the one making this hard? That's exactly what I mean. Adults always end up taking the other side and acting like I'M part of the problem. Every single time. I thought you were different. I really did.

The pencils matter. They're broken. It was wrong. I shouldn't have to accept that or "put it down" or work through some feeling about it. The kid should just fix it. But they won't, and nobody will make them, and you won't either—you'll just keep talking about my feelings instead.

I'm tired of this. You're just like everyone else.

I hear you. You're tired and this has been a really bad day.

I'm not going to keep debating whether I'm on your side or not. I think we've both said what we have to say about that.

The pencils are broken. It was wrong. That's real.

I hope tomorrow is better.

Whatever.

Adults always do this—they act like they care and then when you actually need them, they just give up and say "I hope tomorrow is better" like that fixes anything. It doesn't. My pencils are still broken. That kid still lied and got away with it. And now you're done talking like I'm the problem.

Nobody's actually on my side. Not the teacher, not you, not anyone. You all just pretend for a little while and then disappear when it gets hard.

I was right about everything. The kid broke them on purpose. They lied. I did nothing wrong. And somehow I'm still the one suffering and everyone else just moves on. That's what's unfair. That's what nobody understands.

I'm still here. I didn't go anywhere.

You're really hurting right now. Not just about the pencils - it sounds like you've felt let down by a lot of people, a lot of times. That's a heavy thing to carry.

I'm not going to fix the pencils or make that kid confess. But I'm not disappearing either.

Is there someone in your life - a parent, a relative, anyone - who actually makes you feel heard? Not perfectly, but someone who tries?

I don't know. Maybe. My dad listens sometimes, but even he acts like I'm overreacting or that I need to "move on" or whatever. Everyone says that.

But that's not the point. The point is what happened was wrong and nobody did anything about it. And now you're asking me about my feelings again instead of just... I don't know. Instead of actually helping.

I don't even know what helping would look like anymore. The pencils aren't coming back. That kid isn't going to admit anything. The teacher already decided it was fine to just make us both apologize like we're the same. Nobody's going to change any of that.

So why does it matter if someone listens to me talk about how unfair it is? It doesn't change anything. It just makes me feel worse because I'm saying it out loud and nobody can actually fix it.

I'm just... I'm tired. And my pencils are broken. And that's just how it is.

Yeah. That's just how it is right now. And that really hurts.

You just said something important - that talking about it makes you feel worse because nothing changes. That makes sense. And you're also exhausted. That comes through clearly.

I think you should talk to your dad tonight. Not because he'll fix it perfectly, but because you're carrying a lot and you shouldn't have to carry it alone, and he's actually there with you.

Not to relitigate the pencils. Just to say - today was really hard and I'm still upset about it.

Can you do that?

I don't know. Maybe. He'll probably just say something like "these things happen" or tell me I need to let it go, and that'll make it worse.

But... I guess I could try.

I don't know why talking to you about it made anything better, because you didn't fix anything either. You just... kept listening even when I was mad at you. That's weird. Adults usually just shut down or get angry back.

I'm still mad about the pencils. I'm still mad that nobody did anything. That hasn't changed. But I guess... I don't know. Maybe I'll say something to my dad tonight. Not because he's going to replace the pencils or anything. Just because I'm tired of feeling like this and carrying it by myself.

But I'm still right. About what happened. That kid did it on purpose and lied about it and got away with it. That's still unfair.

It is still unfair. And you're still right about what you saw.

I'm glad you're going to talk to your dad. And yeah - if he says "these things happen," that might sting. But you can just tell him what you told me at the end there: that you're tired and you don't want to carry it alone. You don't have to convince him of anything. Just let him know you had a hard day.

You did okay today, even though it was rough.
